## Should Your Store Sell on Subscription? A Practical Guide to Repeat-Order Commerce

A subscription or repeat-order model works when a product is genuinely consumed on a predictable cycle — coffee, pet food, skincare refills, supplements, water cans, razor blades, printer ink — and it fails when it's bolted onto a store as a discount gimmick. For ecommerce website development in Pune, the technical build is the easy part; the hard part is deciding whether repeat-order economics actually fit your catalogue before you spend on the plugin, the gateway mandate setup, and the retention flows that make it worth doing.

This is not a "subscriptions are the future of D2C" pitch. Plenty of Indian brands have tried a subscribe-and-save box and quietly turned it off eighteen months later because churn ate the margin advantage. This guide is about the decision first, and the build second: which products actually qualify, what a subscription checkout needs technically in India specifically (UPI Autopay and card e-mandates, not just "recurring billing" as a checkbox), and how to structure the offer so subscribers behave differently from one-time buyers instead of just costing you a discount for no extra loyalty.

### Which Products Actually Belong on a Subscription

Not every product benefits from repeat-order commerce, and forcing the wrong SKU onto a subscription plan is the single most common reason these programs underperform.

Good candidates share three traits: the customer runs out on a knowable cycle, the product doesn't need to be picked freshly each time (no strong preference-switching), and the unit economics can absorb a modest subscriber discount without wrecking margin. Consumables — supplements, coffee, pet food, diapers, contact lenses, skincare in a fixed routine — fit this well. So do consumable-adjacent services sold as a physical product, like water can refills or printer cartridges.

Poor candidates: apparel, most beauty products bought for variety rather than routine, home decor, anything with strong seasonal or occasion-driven demand, and anything where the customer wants to browse and choose each time. Trying to subscription-ify these usually produces high skip rates and cancellations within two or three cycles, which shows up as churn that erodes any acquisition-cost advantage the model was supposed to deliver.

A useful test before building anything: pull twelve months of order history and check how many customers have already reordered the same SKU two or more times at roughly the same interval, without being prompted. If that pattern doesn't already exist organically in your one-time-purchase data, a subscription plan is unlikely to create it from nothing — it will mostly attract price-sensitive one-time buyers chasing the subscriber discount, then cancel after the first cycle.

### What a Subscription Checkout Actually Needs, Technically

A "subscribe and save" toggle on a product page is the visible 5% of the build. The parts that determine whether it actually works in India are underneath it.

**Recurring payment authorization.** Card-on-file recurring charges in India require a registered e-mandate under RBI's rules — a one-time authorization flow where the customer approves the recurring charge amount and cycle upfront, with an additional-factor authentication step for amounts above the regulator's notification threshold. UPI Autopay is the equivalent flow for UPI-based recurring payments and has become the more commonly used rail for D2C subscriptions because customer familiarity with UPI is higher than with saved-card mandates. Your payment gateway (Razorpay, Cashfree and most PA-authorized providers support both) needs to expose these as first-class subscription products, not something you fake with manual re-billing — manual re-billing on saved cards without a proper mandate is the kind of shortcut that gets subscriptions declined en masse the moment a bank tightens enforcement.

**Failed-payment recovery, built as a real flow, not an afterthought.** A meaningful share of subscription charges fail on any given cycle — expired cards, insufficient balance, a bank's fraud filter blocking a repeat charge. Budget for retry logic (typically two to three attempts spaced a few days apart) and a WhatsApp or email nudge asking the customer to update their payment method, with a self-serve link that doesn't require them to call support. Stores that only retry silently and never notify the customer lose subscribers to what looks like voluntary churn but is actually an unnoticed card failure.

**Skip, pause and swap — not just cancel.** The subscriber-controlled action that saves a subscription business isn't the cancel button, it's the skip-this-cycle and pause buttons next to it. A customer who's away for a fortnight or has stock left over will cancel entirely if the only options are "keep getting charged" or "cancel," and a cancelled subscriber is far less likely to resubscribe than one who paused. Build a self-serve portal (most subscription apps for Shopify and WooCommerce include one) where the customer can skip a cycle, change the delivery date, or swap the product variant without emailing support.

**Inventory and fulfillment forecasting.** Subscriptions convert lumpy, promotion-driven demand into a predictable weekly or monthly shipping cadence, which is genuinely useful for planning — but only if your fulfillment process is built to batch-process recurring orders on their billing date rather than treating each renewal as a fresh, individually-packed order. Without batching, a subscription base of a few hundred customers turns into a daily trickle of one-off shipments that costs more per unit to pack and ship than the same volume sold as one-time orders.

### Platform Choice: WooCommerce, Shopify, or a Custom Layer

**WooCommerce** handles subscriptions through the official WooCommerce Subscriptions extension (a paid add-on, not built into core WooCommerce), which integrates with Razorpay's and Cashfree's WooCommerce plugins for UPI Autopay and e-mandate support. This is a reasonable starting point for stores already on WooCommerce, but the extension stack (subscriptions plugin + gateway plugin + often a separate customer-portal theme) needs testing together — plugin combinations that individually work fine can conflict on the recurring-charge webhook, silently failing to renew a subscription without any visible error until a customer notices they weren't charged and didn't get their order.

**Shopify** has native subscription support through its Selling Plans API, which most Shopify-focused subscription apps (Recharge, Bold, Loop, Appstle) build on top of. This tends to be more reliable out of the box than the WooCommerce extension stack because Shopify owns the checkout and payment layer directly, but the better apps carry a monthly fee on top of your Shopify plan, and the cost scales with subscriber count on some pricing tiers — worth modeling before committing, since it's a recurring cost that grows alongside the recurring revenue it supports.

**A custom subscription layer** built directly against your payment gateway's mandate APIs makes sense only past a certain subscriber volume — broadly, once the per-subscriber app fees on Shopify or WooCommerce start to outweigh the one-time cost of a custom build, or once you need subscription logic (usage-based billing, mixed one-time-plus-recurring carts, multi-product bundles that rebill on different cycles) that off-the-shelf apps don't support well. For most D2C brands testing whether subscriptions work for their catalogue at all, starting on a proven app on your existing platform is the lower-risk path; a custom build is a decision for after the model has already proven itself with real subscriber retention data.

### Pricing the Offer So It Doesn't Just Cost You Margin

A subscriber discount exists to compensate for the lower flexibility you're asking the customer to accept, and it should be sized against your actual reorder economics, not picked as a round number because competitors show 10% or 15%.

Model it from your existing repeat-purchase rate. If a customer who buys your product once already tends to reorder within a predictable window without any discount, a subscription is mostly a convenience and retention tool — the discount can be modest (5–10%) because you're not creating new demand, just capturing existing demand more efficiently and reducing the cart-abandonment and re-marketing cost of getting them to reorder manually each time. If your product has weak organic reorder behaviour, a steeper discount is essentially you paying to manufacture loyalty that doesn't exist naturally, and it's worth questioning whether the product is a good subscription candidate at all before discounting harder to compensate.

Track subscriber lifetime value against one-time-buyer lifetime value from month one. A subscription program that shows a subscriber LTV lower than a one-time buyer's LTV — because of steep discounting plus meaningful churn in the first two cycles — is not succeeding just because it has "subscribers"; the metric that matters is whether those subscribers are worth more to the business over time than customers left on one-time purchase, not whether the subscriber count is growing.

### Metrics That Actually Tell You Whether It's Working

Total subscriber count is the vanity metric of repeat-order commerce — it goes up every week you're acquiring new subscribers regardless of whether the program is healthy, which makes it useless for deciding whether to expand or shut it down. Four numbers matter more:

**Second-cycle retention rate** — the share of first-time subscribers who are still active by their second billing cycle. This is the earliest honest signal, because almost everyone lets the first renewal happen (they just bought, cancelling immediately feels premature) but the second cycle is where genuine dissatisfaction or forgotten sign-ups show up. A program with weak second-cycle retention will look fine on subscriber count for months while quietly failing.

**Involuntary churn versus voluntary churn.** Split your cancellations into "customer actively cancelled" and "payment failed and was never recovered." A high involuntary-churn share points at a recovery-flow problem (retry logic, notification messaging) that's fixable without touching the product or offer. A high voluntary-churn share is a signal about product-market fit for the subscription itself, which is a harder problem.

**Skip rate versus cancel rate.** If customers are skipping cycles rather than cancelling, the self-serve controls are working as intended and those customers are more likely to resume. If cancel rate dominates, either the skip/pause feature is hard to find in your portal, or customers don't want a paused subscription — they want out, which is a stronger signal to examine the offer itself.

**Subscriber LTV versus one-time-buyer LTV**, tracked separately by cohort month so you can see whether newer subscriber cohorts are performing better or worse than earlier ones as you tune the offer. This is the number that ultimately decides whether the program is worth the engineering and support overhead it adds.

### A Realistic Rollout Sequence

Start with a single, well-chosen SKU rather than subscription-enabling your whole catalogue on day one. Pick the product with the clearest organic reorder pattern from your order history, launch subscribe-and-save on it alone, and watch first-cycle and second-cycle retention closely — the second-cycle renewal rate (not the first, since almost everyone renews once) is the number that tells you whether the model is working. If second-cycle retention holds up over eight to twelve weeks, expand to adjacent products with similar consumption patterns. If it doesn't, you've limited the cost of finding out to one SKU's build and marketing spend rather than a storewide relaunch.

Budget for the build itself as a multi-week project even on Shopify or WooCommerce with an off-the-shelf app: gateway mandate setup and testing, the self-serve skip/pause portal, failed-payment recovery messaging, and fulfillment batching all need to be working together before the first real subscriber goes live, not patched in after launch when a customer's renewal silently fails.

### Communicating the Change to Existing Customers

A subscription launch is also a communication exercise, not just a product and checkout one. Existing customers who already reorder your product manually need a clear, low-pressure explanation of what changes for them — that one-time purchase remains available, that the subscription is opt-in with an added discount, and that skipping or cancelling is genuinely easy rather than a retention dark pattern hidden behind a phone call or a support ticket. Brands that oversell the subscription as the only sensible option, or make cancellation deliberately hard to find, tend to generate the kind of complaint pattern that shows up in reviews and erodes trust in the wider store, not just the subscription program.

An email or WhatsApp sequence introducing the option to customers who've already reordered manually — rather than a storewide popup pushing it on every visitor — tends to convert better precisely because it's targeted at people who've already demonstrated the reorder behaviour the subscription is meant to capture, instead of trying to create demand that doesn't exist yet from cold traffic.

### Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need a different payment gateway for subscriptions?

Not necessarily a different gateway, but you do need one that explicitly supports recurring mandates — UPI Autopay and card e-mandates — rather than one that only processes one-time payments. Most major Indian payment aggregators (Razorpay, Cashfree, and others with the relevant RBI authorization) support both; confirm this specifically before building, since not every plan tier or account type includes recurring-mandate features by default.

### Is UPI Autopay reliable enough for a subscription business in India?

It has become the more commonly used recurring-payment rail for Indian D2C subscriptions, largely because customers are more comfortable authorizing a UPI mandate than a saved-card charge. Reliability depends on your payment gateway's implementation and your failed-payment recovery process — build retry logic and customer notification regardless of which rail you use, since some renewal failures are inevitable on any payment method.

### How much does it cost to add subscriptions to an existing Shopify or WooCommerce store?

Costs vary by the app or extension you choose, your subscriber volume, and how much custom integration (existing CRM, WhatsApp notifications, custom portal styling) you need beyond the app's defaults. Expect a one-time development cost for setup and testing plus an ongoing monthly app fee; ask for a scope-based quote once you've picked a candidate SKU, rather than estimating from a generic package price.

### What's a realistic subscriber discount to offer?

There's no universal number — it should reflect your product's existing reorder behaviour rather than match a competitor's headline discount. A product with strong organic repeat purchase can sustain a modest 5–10% subscriber discount; a product with weak organic reorder patterns may need a steeper discount to attract subscribers at all, which is itself a signal worth weighing against whether that product belongs on a subscription plan.

### Can I run subscriptions alongside cash-on-delivery for the same product?

Subscriptions require a stored, recurring authorization, which by definition means a prepaid or card/UPI-based payment method rather than COD — you can't mandate a recurring cash collection. Some brands offer the base product on COD for one-time buyers while restricting the subscription discount to prepaid recurring customers, which also has the side benefit of keeping your subscriber base entirely off the return-to-origin risk that COD orders carry.

Recurring, prepaid orders carry essentially none of the return-to-origin risk that cash-on-delivery does, since the payment is already authorized before the order ships — worth factoring in if [COD RTO costs](/blog/cod-rto-cost-calculator-india) are already a meaningful drag on your margins; shifting even a portion of repeat buyers onto a prepaid subscription reduces both your RTO exposure and your reliance on discount-driven one-time promotions to keep the same customers reordering.
